Headline: Moratorium proposed
What happened: The U.S. Forest Service Chief announces plans to develop a transportation policy for the National Forest System. He also proposes an 18-month road building moratorium on 130 National Forests while the policy is developed.

Headline: Moratorium takes effect
What happened: A temporary roadbuilding moratorium takes effect.

Headline: Roadless Rule published
What happened: The USDA publishes the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, generally prohibiting road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting on 58.5 million acres of undeveloped national forest lands, subject to exceptions.

Headline: Rule delayed
What happened: In accordance with President Bush's Regulatory Review Plan, the Roadless Rule is delayed for an additional 60 calendar days.

Headline: Idaho court blocks the rule
What happened: Idaho Federal Judge Edward Lodge issues a preliminary injunction barring the Roadless Rule from taking effect.
Citation: Kootenai Tribe of Idaho v. Veneman, No. CV01-10-N-EJL, 2001 WL 1141275, at *2 (D. Idaho May 10, 2001)

Headline: Ninth Circuit reinstates the rule
What happened: The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals reverses Judge Lodge’s preliminary injunction, reinstating the Roadless Rule.
Citation: Kootenai Tribe of Idaho v. Veneman, 313 F.3d 1094, 1126 (9th Cir. 2002)

Headline: Alaska settlement
What happened: The Bush Administration announces it will settle a lawsuit brought by the State of Alaska by agreeing to propose a temporary exemption for the Tongass National Forest. Separately, it announces it will consider whether the Tongass and Chugach National Forests should be exempted from the Roadless Rule.
Area affected: Tongass and Chugach National Forests, Alaska
Citation: U.S. Dep't of Agric., Release No. 0200.03 (June 9, 2003); see also 68 Fed. Reg. 75,136, 75,136–75,137 (Dec. 30, 2003)

Headline: Wyoming court strikes the rule
What happened: Wyoming Federal Court Judge Clarence Brimmer finds the Roadless Rule illegal and issues an injunction barring it from taking effect.
Citation: Wyoming v. U.S. Dep't of Agric., 277 F. Supp. 2d 1197, 1239 (D. Wyo. 2003)

Headline: Tongass temporarily exempted
What happened: USDA publishes a final rule temporarily exempting the Tongass National Forest from the Roadless Rule.

Headline: Tongass exemption takes effect
What happened: The Tongass exemption takes effect.
Citation: 68 Fed. Reg. 75,136 (Dec. 30, 2003) (effective Jan. 29, 2004)

Headline: State Petitions Rule
What happened: The Bush Administration announces the State Petitions Rule as a substitute for the Roadless Rule, allowing governors to petition for state-specific management requirements.

Headline: Eastern state petitions approved
What happened: The Bush Administration approves petitions from the governors of three Eastern states—Virginia, North Carolina, and South Carolina—concerning state-specific roadless protections for roughly 555,000 acres of forested land within their borders.
Area affected: Virginia, North Carolina and South Carolina (about 555,000 acres)
Citation: Pamela Baldwin & Ross Gorte, Cong. Rsch. Serv., RL30647, The National Forest System Roadless Areas Initiative 31 & nn.122–123 (updated Sept. 7, 2006)

Headline: Court reinstates the Roadless Rule
What happened: Federal District Court Judge Elizabeth Laporte in San Francisco orders reinstatement of the Clinton-era Roadless Rule for almost 50 million acres of national forests and grasslands, generally restricting road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting, subject to exceptions.
Citation: California ex rel. Lockyer v. U.S. Dep't of Agric., No. C05-03508 EDL (N.D. Cal. Sept. 20, 2006), amended, 459 F. Supp. 2d 874, 919 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 11, 2006)

Headline: Final injunction issued
What happened: Judge Laporte issues a final injunction, clarifying its application to certain post-May 2005 oil-and-gas authorizations.
Citation: California ex rel. Lockyer v. U.S. Dep't of Agric., Nos. C05-03508 EDL & C05-04038 EDL, Final Injunction Order, Dkt. 235, at 2–3 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 6, 2007)

Headline: Wyoming court strikes the rule again
What happened: Wyoming Federal District Court Judge Brimmer issues a second decision, very similar to his 2003 decision, invalidating and enjoining the Roadless Rule nationwide.
Citation: Wyoming v. U.S. Dep't of Agric., 570 F. Supp. 2d 1309, 1354–1355 (D. Wyo. 2008)

Headline: Idaho Roadless Rule adopted
What happened: The Forest Service adopts the Idaho Roadless Rule.

Headline: Injunction narrowed
What happened: Judge Laporte partially stays her injunction, limiting geographic scope to the Ninth Circuit and New Mexico.
Area affected: Ninth Circuit states and New Mexico
Citation: California ex rel. Lockyer v. U.S. Dep't of Agric., Nos. C05-03508 EDL & C05-04038 EDL, Order Partially Staying Injunctive Relief, Dkt. 283 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 2, 2008)

Headline: Colorado rule postponed
What happened: Colorado and Administration officials agree to postpone action on the proposed Colorado Roadless Rule until spring 2009.
Citation: Colorado Secures Delay in Implementation of Roadless Management Plan, Am. Whitewater (Dec. 5, 2008)

Headline: Ninth Circuit upholds the rule
What happened: The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals upholds Roadless Rule restrictions affecting over 40 million acres of national forests and grasslands, generally limiting road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting.
Area affected: Ninth Circuit states and New Mexico
Citation: California ex rel. Lockyer v. U.S. Dep't of Agric., 575 F.3d 999, 1021 (9th Cir. 2009)

Headline: Secretary review extended
What happened: The Obama Administration extends for another year a requirement that certain road construction, road reconstruction, and timber cutting or removal decisions in inventoried roadless areas be reserved to the Secretary of Agriculture.
Citation: U.S. Dep't of Agric., Secretary's Memorandum 1042-155 (May 28, 2010), cited in Kristina Alexander & Ross W. Gorte, Cong. Rsch. Serv., RL30647, National Forest System (NFS) Roadless Area Initiatives 18 n.97 (Apr. 18, 2011)

Headline: Idaho rule upheld
What happened: Idaho District Court upholds the Idaho Roadless Rule.
Citation: Jayne v. Rey, 780 F. Supp. 2d 1099 (D. Idaho 2011)

Headline: Tongass exemption vacated
What happened: Alaska District Court vacates the 2003 Tongass exemption and reinstates the Roadless Rule on the Tongass.
Citation: Organized Village of Kake v. U.S. Dep't of Agric., 776 F. Supp. 2d 960, 976–977 (D. Alaska 2011)

Headline: Tenth Circuit upholds the rule
What happened: The Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals reverses the Wyoming District Court and directs that the prior injunction be vacated.
Citation: Wyoming v. U.S. Dep't of Agric., 661 F.3d 1209, 1272 (10th Cir. 2011)

Headline: Colorado Roadless Rule adopted
What happened: The Forest Service adopts the Colorado Roadless Rule.
Citation: U.S. Forest Serv., Colorado Roadless Rule

Headline: Tongass exemption revived
What happened: A divided panel of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals reverses the 2011 Alaska District Court decision by a 2–1 split vote, reviving the Tongass exemption.
Citation: Organized Village of Kake v. U.S. Dep't of Agric., 746 F.3d 970 (9th Cir. 2014)

Headline: Rehearing en banc granted
What happened: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit announces it will re-hear the case challenging the Tongass exemption. The court grants the rehearing en banc, rendering the earlier opinion ineffective.
Citation: Organized Village of Kake v. U.S. Dep't of Agric., 765 F.3d 1117 (9th Cir. 2014)

Headline: Tongass exemption struck down
What happened: The Ninth Circuit's 11-judge en banc panel rules that the exemption of the Tongass from the Roadless Rule was invalid under the Administrative Procedure Act.
Citation: Organized Village of Kake v. U.S. Dep't of Agric., 795 F.3d 956, 966–970 (9th Cir. 2015) (en banc)

Headline: Alaska rulemaking begins
What happened: Alaska and the Forest Service enter an agreement as cooperating agencies for an Alaska roadless rulemaking after Alaska petitioned for a Tongass exemption.
Citation: Memorandum of Understanding Between the State of Alaska and USDA Forest Service (Aug. 2, 2018)

Headline: Tongass exemption finalized
What happened: The Trump Administration publishes a final rule exempting the Tongass National Forest from the Roadless Rule.

Headline: Tongass protections restored
What happened: The U.S. Forest Service formally reinstates the 2001 Roadless Rule management regime across the Tongass National Forest, reimposing restrictions on road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting, subject to exceptions, across about 9.37 million acres of land.
Area affected: Tongass National Forest, Alaska (about 9.37 million acres)

Headline: Utilities sue USDA
What happened: Represented by Pacific Legal Foundation, Inside Passage Electric Cooperative and Alaska Power Association file suit against USDA after the agency’s January 2023 decision reinstating the 2001 Roadless Rule on the Tongass National Forest. The USDA lacked statutory authority to reimpose the rule, and the restrictions impede hydroelectric, geothermal, and other infrastructure projects that require road access.
Citation: Complaint, Inside Passage Elec. Coop. v. U.S. Dep't of Agric., No. 3:23-cv-00204-SLG (D. Alaska Sept. 8, 2023)

Headline: Executive order on the Tongass
What happened: On his first day in office, President Trump signs an executive order directing the Secretary of Agriculture to reinstate the 2020 Alaska Roadless Rule’s exemption for the Tongass.

Headline: Rescission announced
What happened: Agriculture Secretary Rollins announces USDA’s intention to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule, and USDA begins the formal rulemaking process.
Area affected: Nationwide (Idaho and Colorado keep their own rules)
Citation: U.S. Dep't of Agric., Secretary Rollins Rescinds Roadless Rule, Eliminating Impediment to Responsible Forest Management (June 23, 2025); see also 90 Fed. Reg. 42,179 (Aug. 29, 2025)

Headline: Rescission proposed
What happened: The U.S. Forest Service publishes a proposed rule and environmental review for rescinding the Roadless Rule.
Area affected: Nationwide (Idaho and Colorado keep their own rules)
Citation: 91 Fed. Reg. 53,827–53,832 (Aug. 20, 2026); see also 91 Fed. Reg. 57,841 (Sept. 11, 2026) (extending comment period)
